e-9040.knowledge_point: Reducing a Homogeneous ODE to a First-Order System
e-9040.problem:
The third-order differential equation 

$$
y''' - 3\sqrt{t}\, y'' + t^3 y' - 4t^2 y= 0
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where $x_1(t) = y(t),$ $x_2(t) = y'(t)$ and $x_3(t) = y''(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
e-9040.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1, x_2,$ and $x_3.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $(y'''),$ we obtain

$$
y''' = 3\sqrt{t}\,y'' - t^3 y' + 4t^2 y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
y''' = 3\sqrt{t}\, x_3 - t^3 x_2 + 4t^2 x_1.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=4{t}^{2}\,{x}_{1}-{t}^{3}{x}_{2}+3\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t) = 4t^2 x_1 - t^3 x_2 + 3\sqrt{t} \,x_3.$

e-9041.knowledge_point: Reducing a Homogeneous Initial Value Problem to a First-Order System
e-9041.problem:
The second-order initial value problem

$$
y''  + y' - 6y= 0 , \quad y(0)= 1, \quad y'(0)= 4
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(0)=p \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=f(t),\, & {x}_{2}(0)=q\end{aligned}
$$

where $x_1(t) = y(t),$ $x_2(t) = y'(t),$ and $p$ and $q$ are constants. Calculate  $(p-q)\cdot f(t).$
e-9041.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′}.\end{aligned}
$$

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & ={x}_{1}(0)=1 \\ {y}^{′}(0) & ={x}_{2}(0)=4\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1$ and $x_2.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $(y''),$ we obtain

$$
y'' = - y' + 6y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
y'' = - x_2 + 6x_1.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(0)=1 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=6{x}_{1}-{x}_{2},\, & {x}_{2}(0)=4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $p=1, q=4, f(t) = 6x_1 - x_2,$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}(p-q)\cdot f(t) & =(1-4)(6{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}) \\  & =-3(6{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

e-9138.knowledge_point: Writing a Homogeneous ODE as a Matrix Differential Equation
e-9138.problem:
The second-order differential equation $y'' + 5y' - 2y=0$
can be expressed as the matrix equation $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),$ where 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070402/assets/59e386be8b30fca475a2e0d164687a6561b9ab368b9879fc301d328896d184fd.png)
Find the matrix $A.$
e-9138.worked_solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1$ and $x_2.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $(y''),$ we obtain

$$
y''= -5y' + 2y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
y'' = -5x_2 + 2x_1.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=2{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation $\mathbf x'(t) = A\mathbf x(t)$ as follows:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070402/assets/f35de5e6f066144c4130e38304abbff552730dc1fe97828572a66e68970c5d52.png)

Hence, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070402/assets/314f9dcf277b61dac9985c448aed98113516592e3822cc47a8566d28a480651b.png)

after.problem:
The second-order differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{y}^{′}-10y=0
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{y}^{′}+10y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{2}+10{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=10{x}_{1}+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=10{x}_{1}+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{2}.$

Question 1
?

The second-order differential equation

y″−3sin⁡ty′−10y=0

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

{x1′=x2x2′=f(t) where x1(t)=y(t) and x2(t)=y′(t). Find the function f(t).

a
−10x1−3sin⁡tx2
b
3sin⁡tx1−10x2
c
3sin⁡tx1+10x2
d
−3sin⁡tx1−10x2
e
10x1+3sin⁡tx2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we make the following change of variables: x1=yx2=y′

Differentiating the above equations with respect to t, we get x1′=y′x2′=y″

which we can rewrite as

{x1′=x2,x2′=y″.

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of x1 and x2.

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative (y″), we obtain y″=3sin⁡ty′+10y.

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives y″=3sin⁡tx2+10x1. Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows: {x1′=x2x2′=10x1+3sin⁡tx2

Finally, f(t)=10x1+3sin⁡tx2.

content.knowledge_point: Reducing a Homogeneous ODE to a First-Order System
content.problem:
The second-order differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{y}^{′}-10y=0
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
content.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{y}^{′}+10y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{2}+10{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=10{x}_{1}+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=10{x}_{1}+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{2}.$

before.name: Question 2
before.problem:
The third-order differential equation 

$$
{y}^{‴}+3{t}^{1/2}{y}^{″}-7y=0
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t)$ and ${x}_{3}(t)={y}^{″}(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$

decision.explanation: Since x₃'=y''', rearrange the equation to obtain y'''=7y−3t^{1/2}y''. Substituting y=x₁ and y''=x₃ gives f(t)=7x₁−3t^{1/2}x₃, option d.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
The third-order differential equation 

$$
{y}^{‴}+3{t}^{1/2}{y}^{″}-7y=0
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t)$ and ${x}_{3}(t)={y}^{″}(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=-3{t}^{1/2}{y}^{″}+7y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=-3{t}^{1/2}{x}_{3}+7{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=7{x}_{1}-3{t}^{1/2}{x}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=7{x}_{1}-3{t}^{1/2}{x}_{3}.$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t)$ and ${x}_{3}(t)={y}^{″}(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
content.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=-3{t}^{1/2}{y}^{″}+7y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=-3{t}^{1/2}{x}_{3}+7{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=7{x}_{1}-3{t}^{1/2}{x}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=7{x}_{1}-3{t}^{1/2}{x}_{3}.$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
The second-order differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}-4{e}^{t}{y}^{′}+4ty=0
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=4{e}^{t}{y}^{′}-4ty.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=4{e}^{t}{x}_{2}-4t{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=-4t{x}_{1}+4{e}^{t}{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=-4t{x}_{1}+4{e}^{t}{x}_{2}.$

Question 3
?

The second-order differential equation

y″−4ety′+4ty=0

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

{x1′=x2x2′=f(t) where x1(t)=y(t) and x2(t)=y′(t). Find the function f(t).

a
−4etx1+4tx2
b
−4tx1+4etx2
c
4etx1−4tx2
d
4tx1−4etx2
e
4etx1+4tx2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we make the following change of variables: x1=yx2=y′

Differentiating the above equations with respect to t, we get x1′=y′x2′=y″

which we can rewrite as

{x1′=x2,x2′=y″.

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of x1 and x2.

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative (y″), we obtain y″=4ety′−4ty.

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives y″=4etx2−4tx1. Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows: {x1′=x2x2′=−4tx1+4etx2

Finally, f(t)=−4tx1+4etx2.

content.knowledge_point: Reducing a Homogeneous ODE to a First-Order System
content.problem:
The second-order differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}-4{e}^{t}{y}^{′}+4ty=0
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
content.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=4{e}^{t}{y}^{′}-4ty.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=4{e}^{t}{x}_{2}-4t{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=-4t{x}_{1}+4{e}^{t}{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=-4t{x}_{1}+4{e}^{t}{x}_{2}.$

before.name: Question 4
before.problem:
The third-order differential equation 

$$
{y}^{‴}+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{y}^{″}-{t}^{3}{y}^{′}+2y=0
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ and ${x}_{3}(t)={y}^{″}(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$

Question 4
?

The third-order differential equation y‴+sin⁡ty″−t3y′+2y=0

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

{x1′=x2x2′=x3x3′=f(t) where x1(t)=y(t), x2(t)=y′(t), and x3(t)=y″(t). Find the function f(t).

a
t3x1+sin⁡tx2−2x3
b
sin⁡tx1−t3x2+2x3
c
2x1−t3x2+sin⁡tx3
d
−2x1+t3x2−sin⁡tx3
e
−sin⁡tx1+t3x2−2x3
Submit

decision.explanation: Solving for y''' gives y'''=−sin(t)y''+t³y'−2y. Substituting x₁=y, x₂=y', and x₃=y'' yields f(t)=−2x₁+t³x₂−sin(t)x₃, option d.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
The third-order differential equation 

$$
{y}^{‴}+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{y}^{″}-{t}^{3}{y}^{′}+2y=0
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ and ${x}_{3}(t)={y}^{″}(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{y}^{″}+{t}^{3}{y}^{′}-2y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{3}+{t}^{3}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=-2{x}_{1}+{t}^{3}{x}_{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=-2{x}_{1}+{t}^{3}{x}_{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{3}.$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

{x1′=x2x2′=x3x3′=f(t) where x1(t)=y(t), x2(t)=y′(t), and x3(t)=y″(t). Find the function f(t).

a
t3x1+sin⁡tx2−2x3
b
sin⁡tx1−t3x2+2x3
c
2x1−t3x2+sin⁡tx3
d
−2x1+t3x2−sin⁡tx3
e
−sin⁡tx1+t3x2−2x3
Submit

EXPLANATION

First, we make the following change of variables: x1=yx2=y′x3=y″

Differentiating the above equations with respect to t, we get x1′=y′x2′=y″x3′=y‴

which we can rewrite as

{x1′=x2,x2′=x3,x3′=y‴.

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of x1,x2, and x3.

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative (y‴), we obtain y‴=−sin⁡ty″+t3y′−2y.

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives y‴=−sin⁡tx3+t3x2−2x1. Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows: {x1′=x2x2′=x3x3′=−2x1+t3x2−sin⁡tx3

Finally, f(t)=−2x1+t3x2−sin⁡tx3.

content.knowledge_point: Reducing a Homogeneous ODE to a First-Order System
content.problem:
The third-order differential equation 

$$
{y}^{‴}+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{y}^{″}-{t}^{3}{y}^{′}+2y=0
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ and ${x}_{3}(t)={y}^{″}(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
content.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{y}^{″}+{t}^{3}{y}^{′}-2y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{3}+{t}^{3}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=-2{x}_{1}+{t}^{3}{x}_{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)=-2{x}_{1}+{t}^{3}{x}_{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{3}.$

decision.explanation: Rearranging gives y'''=e^{√t}y−e^t y''. Since x₁=y and x₃=y'', we have x₃'=e^{√t}x₁−e^t x₃, which is option e.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
The third-order differential equation 

$$
{y}^{‴}+{e}^{t}{y}^{″}-{e}^{\sqrt{t}}y=0
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t)$ and ${x}_{3}(t)={y}^{″}(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=-{e}^{t}{y}^{″}+{e}^{\sqrt{t}}y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=-{e}^{t}{x}_{3}+{e}^{\sqrt{t}}{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={e}^{\sqrt{t}}{x}_{1}-{e}^{t}{x}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $f(t)={e}^{\sqrt{t}}{x}_{1}-{e}^{t}{x}_{3}.$

before.problem:
The third-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{‴}-6\sqrt{t}\,{y}^{″}+12{y}^{′}=0,\,y(1)=-2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=2,\,{y}^{″}(1)=-3
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(1)=p \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3},\, & {x}_{2}(1)=q \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=f(t),\, & {x}_{3}(1)=r\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ ${x}_{3}(t)={y}^{″}(t),$ and $p,$ $q$ and $r$ are constants. Calculate  $(p+q-r)\cdot f(t).$

a

decision.explanation: The initial conditions give p=−2, q=2, r=−3, so p+q−r=3. Rearranging the ODE gives f(t)=6√t x₃−12x₂. Thus (p+q−r)f(t)=18√t x₃−36x₂=−18(2x₂−√t x₃), option e.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
The third-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{‴}-6\sqrt{t}\,{y}^{″}+12{y}^{′}=0,\,y(1)=-2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=2,\,{y}^{″}(1)=-3
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(1)=p \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3},\, & {x}_{2}(1)=q \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=f(t),\, & {x}_{3}(1)=r\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ ${x}_{3}(t)={y}^{″}(t),$ and $p,$ $q$ and $r$ are constants. Calculate  $(p+q-r)\cdot f(t).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & ={x}_{1}(1)=-2 \\ {y}^{′}(1) & ={x}_{2}(1)=2 \\ {y}^{″}(1) & ={x}_{3}(1)=-3\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=6\sqrt{t}\,{y}^{″}-12{y}^{′}.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=6\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3}-12{x}_{2}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(1)=-2 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3},\, & {x}_{2}(1)=2 \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=-12{x}_{2}+6\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3},\, & {x}_{3}(1)=-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $p=-2,q=2,r=-3,f(t)=-12{x}_{2}+6\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3},$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}(p+q-r)\cdot f(t) & =(-2+2-(-3))(-12{x}_{2}+6\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3}) \\  & =(-2+2+3)(-12{x}_{2}+6\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3}) \\  & =3(-6)(2{x}_{2}-\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3}) \\  & =-18(2{x}_{2}-\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

The third-order initial value problem y‴−6ty″+12y′=0,y(1)=−2,y′(1)=2,y″(1)=−3 can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

{x1′=x2,x1(1)=px2′=x3,x2(1)=qx3′=f(t),x3(1)=r where x1(t)=y(t), x2(t)=y′(t), x3(t)=y″(t), and p, q and r are constants. Calculate (p+q−r)⋅f(t).

a
−8(6tx2+4x3)
b
−6tx2+3x3
c
−4(6x2−3tx3)
d
6tx2−3x3
e
−18(2x2−tx3)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we make the following change of variables: x1(t)=yx2(t)=y′x3(t)=y″

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

y(1)=x1(1)=−2y′(1)=x2(1)=2y″(1)=x3(1)=−3

Differentiating the above equations with respect to t, we get x1′(t)=y′x2′(t)=y″x3′(t)=y‴

which we can rewrite as

{x1′=x2,x2′=x3,x3′=y‴.

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of x1,x2, and x3.

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative (y‴), we obtain y‴=6ty″−12y′.

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives y‴=6tx3−12x2. Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows: {x1′=x2,x1(1)=−2x2′=x3,x2(1)=2x3′=−12x2+6tx3,x3(1)=−3

Finally, p=−2,q=2,r=−3,f(t)=−12x2+6tx3, and

(p+q−r)⋅f(t)=(−2+2−(−3))(−12x2+6tx3)=(−2+2+3)(−12x2+6tx3)=3(−6)(2x2−tx3)=−18(2x2−tx3).

content.knowledge_point: Reducing a Homogeneous Initial Value Problem to a First-Order System
content.problem:
The third-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{‴}-6\sqrt{t}\,{y}^{″}+12{y}^{′}=0,\,y(1)=-2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=2,\,{y}^{″}(1)=-3
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(1)=p \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3},\, & {x}_{2}(1)=q \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=f(t),\, & {x}_{3}(1)=r\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ ${x}_{3}(t)={y}^{″}(t),$ and $p,$ $q$ and $r$ are constants. Calculate  $(p+q-r)\cdot f(t).$
content.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & ={x}_{1}(1)=-2 \\ {y}^{′}(1) & ={x}_{2}(1)=2 \\ {y}^{″}(1) & ={x}_{3}(1)=-3\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=6\sqrt{t}\,{y}^{″}-12{y}^{′}.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=6\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3}-12{x}_{2}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(1)=-2 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3},\, & {x}_{2}(1)=2 \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=-12{x}_{2}+6\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3},\, & {x}_{3}(1)=-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $p=-2,q=2,r=-3,f(t)=-12{x}_{2}+6\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3},$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}(p+q-r)\cdot f(t) & =(-2+2-(-3))(-12{x}_{2}+6\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3}) \\  & =(-2+2+3)(-12{x}_{2}+6\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3}) \\  & =3(-6)(2{x}_{2}-\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3}) \\  & =-18(2{x}_{2}-\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

{x1′=x2,x1(2)=px2′=f(t),x2(2)=q where x1(t)=y(t), x2(t)=y′(t), and p and q are constants. Calculate (p−q)⋅f(t).

a

b
tx1−4x2
c
3(4x1−tx2)
d
−tx1+4x2
e
−2(4x1−tx2)
Submit

decision.explanation: The initial conditions give p=−2 and q=−3, so p−q=1. Rearranging the ODE gives y''=ty−4y', hence f(t)=tx₁−4x₂. Therefore (p−q)f(t)=tx₁−4x₂, option b.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
The second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}-ty=0,\,y(2)=-2,\,{y}^{′}(2)=-3
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(2)=p \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=f(t),\, & {x}_{2}(2)=q\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ and $p$ and $q$ are constants. Calculate  $(p-q)\cdot f(t).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′}.\end{aligned}
$$

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(2) & ={x}_{1}(2)=-2 \\ {y}^{′}(2) & ={x}_{2}(2)=-3\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=-4{y}^{′}+ty.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=-4{x}_{2}+t{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(2)=-2 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=t{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2},\, & {x}_{2}(2)=-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $p=-2,q=-3,f(t)=t{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2},$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}(p-q)\cdot f(t) & =(-2-(-3))(t{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}) \\  & =(1)(t{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}) \\  & =t{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
The second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-3{y}^{′}+2y=0,\,y(1)=2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=3
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(1)=p \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=f(t),\, & {x}_{2}(1)=q\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ and $p$ and $q$ are constants. Calculate  $(p-q)\cdot f(t).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′}.\end{aligned}
$$

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & ={x}_{1}(1)=2 \\ {y}^{′}(1) & ={x}_{2}(1)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=3{y}^{′}-2y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=3{x}_{2}-2{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(1)=2 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=-2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2},\, & {x}_{2}(1)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $p=2,q=3,f(t)=-2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2},$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}(p-q)\cdot f(t) & =(2-3)f(t) \\  & =-f(t) \\  & =2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Reducing a Homogeneous Initial Value Problem to a First-Order System
content.problem:
The second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-3{y}^{′}+2y=0,\,y(1)=2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=3
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(1)=p \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=f(t),\, & {x}_{2}(1)=q\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ and $p$ and $q$ are constants. Calculate  $(p-q)\cdot f(t).$
content.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′}.\end{aligned}
$$

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & ={x}_{1}(1)=2 \\ {y}^{′}(1) & ={x}_{2}(1)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=3{y}^{′}-2y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=3{x}_{2}-2{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(1)=2 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=-2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2},\, & {x}_{2}(1)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $p=2,q=3,f(t)=-2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2},$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}(p-q)\cdot f(t) & =(2-3)f(t) \\  & =-f(t) \\  & =2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
The third-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{‴}+3{y}^{″}-4{y}^{′}-12y=0,\,y(0)=2,\,{y}^{′}(0)=1,\,{y}^{″}(0)=3
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(0)=p \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3},\, & {x}_{2}(0)=q \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=f(t),\, & {x}_{3}(0)=r\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ ${x}_{3}(t)={y}^{″}(t),$ and $p,$ $q$ and $r$ are constants. Calculate  $(p-q+r)\cdot f(t).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & ={x}_{1}(0)=2 \\ {y}^{′}(0) & ={x}_{2}(0)=1 \\ {y}^{″}(0) & ={x}_{3}(0)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=-3{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}+12y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=-3{x}_{3}+4{x}_{2}+12{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(0)=2 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3},\, & {x}_{2}(0)=1 \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=12{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3},\, & {x}_{3}(0)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $p=2,q=1,r=3,f(t)=12{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3},$ and 

$$

The third-order initial value problem y‴+3y″−4y′−12y=0,y(0)=2,y′(0)=1,y″(0)=3 can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

{x1′=x2,x1(0)=px2′=x3,x2(0)=qx3′=f(t),x3(0)=r where x1(t)=y(t), x2(t)=y′(t), x3(t)=y″(t), and p, q and r are constants. Calculate (p−q+r)⋅f(t).

a
4(−3x1+4x2+12x3)
b
5(3x1−4x2−12x3)
c
2(12x1+4x2−3x3)
d
4(12x1+4x2−3x3)
e
4(−12x1−4x2+3x3)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we make the following change of variables: x1(t)=yx2(t)=y′x3(t)=y″

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

y(0)=x1(0)=2y′(0)=x2(0)=1y″(0)=x3(0)=3

Differentiating the above equations with respect to t, we get x1′(t)=y′x2′(t)=y″x3′(t)=y‴

which we can rewrite as

{x1′=x2,x2′=x3,x3′=y‴.

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of x1,x2, and x3.

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative (y‴), we obtain y‴=−3y″+4y′+12y.

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives y‴=−3x3+4x2+12x1. Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows: {x1′=x2,x1(0)=2x2′=x3,x2(0)=1x3′=12x1+4x2−3x3,x3(0)=3

Finally, p=2,q=1,r=3,f(t)=12x1+4x2−3x3, and

(p−q+r)⋅f(t)=(2−1+3)(12x1+4x2−3x3)=4(12x1+4x2−3x3).

content.knowledge_point: Reducing a Homogeneous Initial Value Problem to a First-Order System
content.problem:
The third-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{‴}+3{y}^{″}-4{y}^{′}-12y=0,\,y(0)=2,\,{y}^{′}(0)=1,\,{y}^{″}(0)=3
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(0)=p \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3},\, & {x}_{2}(0)=q \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=f(t),\, & {x}_{3}(0)=r\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ ${x}_{3}(t)={y}^{″}(t),$ and $p,$ $q$ and $r$ are constants. Calculate  $(p-q+r)\cdot f(t).$
content.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & ={x}_{1}(0)=2 \\ {y}^{′}(0) & ={x}_{2}(0)=1 \\ {y}^{″}(0) & ={x}_{3}(0)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=-3{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}+12y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=-3{x}_{3}+4{x}_{2}+12{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(0)=2 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3},\, & {x}_{2}(0)=1 \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=12{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3},\, & {x}_{3}(0)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $p=2,q=1,r=3,f(t)=12{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3},$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}(p-q+r)\cdot f(t) & =(2-1+3)(12{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}) \\  & =4(12{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where

Question 11
?

The second-order differential equation 3y″+9sin⁡ty′+y=0 can be expressed as the matrix equation x′(t)=Ax(t), where

x(t)=[x1x2],A=[abcd],y(t)=x1(t),y′(t)=x2(t). Find the matrix A.

a
[−sin⁡t3−301]
b
[01−13−3sin⁡t]
c
[10−sin⁡t3−3]
d
[01−3sin⁡t−13]
e
[0sin⁡t−130]
Submit

decision.explanation: Since x₁=y and x₂=y', we have x₁'=x₂. Dividing the ODE by 3 gives x₂'=−x₁/3−3sin(t)x₂. These coefficients form the rows of A, so option b is correct.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
The second-order differential equation $3{y}^{″}+9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{y}^{′}+y=0$
can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where 

$$
x(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}],\,y(t)={x}_{1}(t),\,{y}^{′}(t)={x}_{2}(t).
$$

Find the matrix $A.$
after.worked_solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{y}^{′}-\frac{1}{3}y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{2}-\frac{1}{3}{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=-\frac{1}{3}{x}_{1}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -\frac{1}{3} & -3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Hence, $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -\frac{1}{3} & -3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].$

x(t)=[x1x2],A=[abcd],y(t)=x1(t),y′(t)=x2(t). Find the matrix A.

a
[−sin⁡t3−301]
b
[01−13−3sin⁡t]
c
[10−sin⁡t3−3]

[01−3sin⁡t−13]

[0sin⁡t−130]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables: x1=yx2=y′

Differentiating the above equations with respect to t, we get x1′=y′x2′=y″

which we can rewrite as

{x1′=x2,x2′=y″.

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of x1 and x2.

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative (y″), we obtain y″=−3sin⁡ty′−13y.

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives y″=−3sin⁡tx2−13x1. Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows: {x1′=x2x2′=−13x1−3sin⁡tx2

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation x′(t)=Ax(t) as follows: [x1′x2′]=[01−13−3sin⁡t][x1x2].

Hence, A=[01−13−3sin⁡t].

content.knowledge_point: Writing a Homogeneous ODE as a Matrix Differential Equation
content.problem:
The second-order differential equation $3{y}^{″}+9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{y}^{′}+y=0$
can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where 

$$
x(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}],\,y(t)={x}_{1}(t),\,{y}^{′}(t)={x}_{2}(t).
$$

Find the matrix $A.$
content.worked_solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{y}^{′}-\frac{1}{3}y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{2}-\frac{1}{3}{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=-\frac{1}{3}{x}_{1}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -\frac{1}{3} & -3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

history.worked_solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{y}^{′}-\frac{1}{3}y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{2}-\frac{1}{3}{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=-\frac{1}{3}{x}_{1}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -\frac{1}{3} & -3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Hence, $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -\frac{1}{3} & -3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].$

after.worked_solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=-5{y}^{″}+3{t}^{2}{y}^{′}.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=-5{x}_{3}+3{t}^{2}{x}_{2}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=3{t}^{2}{x}_{2}-5{x}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 3{t}^{2} & -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

Hence, $a=3{t}^{2},b=1,c=-5,$ and $a+b+c=3{t}^{2}-4.$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=3{y}^{′}-4y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=3{x}_{2}-4{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=-4{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -4 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

Hence, $a=-4,b=1,c=3,$ and $a+b+c=0.$

We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=3{y}^{′}-4y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=3{x}_{2}-4{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=-4{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -4 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

Hence, $a=-4,b=1,c=3,$ and $a+b+c=0.$

\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=4{y}^{′}-3y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=4{x}_{2}-3{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=-3{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Hence, $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}].$

content.problem:
The second-order differential equation ${y}^{″}-4{y}^{′}+3y=0$
can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where 

$$
x(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}],\,y(t)={x}_{1}(t),\,{y}^{′}(t)={x}_{2}(t).
$$

Find the matrix $A.$
content.worked_solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=4{y}^{′}-3y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=4{x}_{2}-3{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=-3{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Hence, $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}].$
